Retroactive Advantage Correction:
Closed-Form V-Trace Bias Correction
for Delay-Aware RLHF

Arnav Raj Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, New Delhi, India Correspondence to: arnav.raj.cs522@cse.iitd.ac.in
Abstract

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in production does not always have a synchronous reward signal. Code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, and queued human review can return several gradient steps after the rollout that produced them, breaking the synchronous-reward assumption underlying standard PPO. We address this gap with Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC): each pending slow completion is queued, aged through a non-negative kernel, and reinjected as a clipped residual into the next optimiser step’s advantage. We prove that under an unbiased clipped importance ratio, the cumulative RAC correction is exactly unbiased when the effective delay kernel reinjects all of its mass, and carries a bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise; at the no-delay identity kernel it reduces to V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018). On a tabular Markov decision process (MDP) proof-of-concept, RAC reduces the closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9×\bm{47.9\times} at the two-slow-channel configuration, beating wait-for-slow at lower wall-clock cost. RAC integrates with PPO and GRPO through a two-line reward-manager patch.

Keywords: 
RLHF, delay-aware reinforcement learning, V-trace, bias correction, off-policy correction, asynchronous training

1 Introduction

Delayed rewards in deployed RLHF.

Standard PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) implicitly assumes that the reward rtr_{t} for trajectory τt\tau_{t} is observed before the optimiser commits its next gradient on πθ\pi_{\theta}. That assumption holds for simulated rollouts but is not always met in deployed RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022): code-execution verifiers return several gradient steps after the rollout that produced them (Jain et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026); slow but accurate 7070B judge ensembles run on a different clock from a fast 77B PRISM-style scorer (Kirk et al., 2024); human review of edge cases returns minutes later, after the policy has already moved; and asynchronous training architectures such as AReaL (Fu et al., 2025) and Asynchronous RLHF (Noukhovitch et al., 2025) explicitly decouple inference workers from learners, making Δ\Delta-step staleness (where Δ\Delta is the gradient-step lag) a first-class operational parameter. When the slow signal arrives Δ\Delta steps late and is dropped, the bias accumulates with Δ\Delta and with the number KK of distinct slow channels (e.g. a code-verifier plus a judge-RM is K=2K{=}2).11 1 Code: https://github.com/deadsmash07/rac-rlxf-code.

Off-policy correctors and the reward axis.

V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018) and Retrace (Munos et al., 2016) are clipped importance-sampling (IS) correctors for off-policy value-function targets, acting on the inner critic and addressing inter-worker actor staleness, not the inter-optimiser-step reward delay we target. Recent IS-clipping work tightens the off-policy PPO objective at the token or turn level: CISPO (Chen et al., 2025) clips the per-token ratio while preserving gradients; Truncated PPO (Fan et al., 2025) extends generalised advantage estimation (Schulman et al., 2016) onto truncated rollouts; and SORL (Li et al., 2025a) adds turn-level IS clipping with clipping-triggered normalisation. The 20252025–20262026 staleness-aware-PPO cluster (Zheng et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b; Xi et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Sheng et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025) acts on the rollout-axis IS ratio at the token or sequence level. Prior delayed-reward correctors operate on a different axis. RUDDER (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019) redistributes a terminal episodic reward backward within an episode, a credit-assignment construction; Han et al. (2022) reformulate the QQ-function for single-channel delayed reward in continuous control; Zhang et al. (2023) cover per-agent reward delays in tabular multi-agent RL with cooperative convergence-rate guarantees; Ramstedt et al. (2021) resample trajectory fragments in hindsight for action-delay and observation-delay MDPs; and AReaL (Fu et al., 2025) with Asynchronous RLHF (Noukhovitch et al., 2025) bound generation staleness empirically by capping how off-policy each inference worker can drift. RAC occupies a third axis. Each slow reward that arrives Δ\Delta optimiser steps late is queued and reinjected as an additive advantage correction at the next optimiser step, weighted by an age kernel and a clipped IS ratio. Across KK slow channels these reinjections pass through a row-stochastic delay kernel, which makes the cumulative bias closed-form zero in expectation (Theorem 2.1) and recovers V-trace’s on-policy guarantee at the identity kernel.

RAC at a glance.

Figure 1 sketches the mechanism. Standard PPO commits its gradient before the slow channel returns and drops the residual signal. RAC instead treats the late slow return as evidence about an earlier rollout: it queues the pending slow completion, ages it through a non-negative kernel wage​(Δ)w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta), and reinjects the slow-minus-fast residual into the next gradient, weighted by a clipped IS ratio. The clip is the standard off-policy correction taken from V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018) and transplanted from the value-target level to the advantage level. The construction is a multi-channel Δ\Delta-step lag accumulator constrained by a row-stochastic delay kernel. The cumulative bias of the correction is linear in the row-stochasticity slack of the effective kernel, and is exactly zero in expectation at the saturated case (Theorem 2.1). At the identity kernel Λ=I\Lambda{=}I (zero delay), Theorem 2.1 collapses to V-trace’s on-policy guarantee, and the technical contribution is the closed-form multi-channel Δ\Delta-lagged extension.

Contributions.

The paper makes two contributions.

  • •

    (C1) Closed-form cumulative-bias identity. Under the V-trace conditional-independence condition, the cumulative RAC correction has bias linear in the row-stochasticity slack η\eta of the effective delay kernel, and is exact (η=0\eta\!=\!0) at the saturated kernel and at the V-trace identity kernel (Theorem 2.1, Espeholt et al., 2018). A total-variation bound combining Pinsker’s inequality (Canonne, 2022) with the Bretagnolle–Huber lemma (Bretagnolle & Huber, 1979) (Proposition 2.2) supplies per-step divergence control.

  • •

    (C2) Tabular MDP proof-of-concept and 𝟕\bm{7}B-scale verifications. On a 3×23{\times}2 tabular MDP RAC reduces closed-form policy bias by 47.9×\bm{47.9\times} at the K=2K{=}2 configuration, with single-step wall-clock cost (Table 1, Figure 2). Three machine-precision 77B-scale checks corroborate the identity-kernel collapse, the linear-in-slack bias scaling, and V-trace equivalence on real reward distributions (Appendix B, Appendix G).

2 Method: Retroactive Advantage Correction

Setup.

At optimiser step tt a rollout τt=(st,0,at,0,…,st,T−1,at,T−1)\tau_{t}=(s_{t,0},a_{t,0},\dots,s_{t,T-1},a_{t,T-1}) produces, for each index ii, a fast reward estimate rt,ifast∈ℝr^{\mathrm{fast}}_{t,i}\in\mathbb{R} returned synchronously. A slow channel kk returns a verifier-graded reward rt,islow,kr^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i} at step t+Δkt+\Delta_{k}, where Δk∈{0,1,2,…}\Delta_{k}\!\in\!\{0,1,2,\ldots\} is a channel-specific lag (the Δk=0\Delta_{k}{=}0 boundary recovers synchronous reward and is the V-trace identity-kernel case). The fast baseline rt,ifast,blr^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}_{t,i} is either the fast estimate itself or a GRPO-style (Shao et al., 2024) leave-one-out variant. We assume the slow residual rt,islow,k−rt,ifast,blr^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i}{-}r^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}_{t,i} has bounded variance σs2\sigma_{s}^{2} uniformly across (t,k,i)(t,k,i), and the policy KL satisfies KLt=𝔼[KL(πt∥π~t)]<∞\mathrm{KL}_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{t}\|\widetilde{\pi}_{t})]<\infty.

The RAC primitive.

RAC maintains a queue QQ of pending slow completions. When rt,islow,kr^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i} returns at step t+Δkt+\Delta_{k}, it is forward-injected into the advantage of step t+Δk+1t+\Delta_{k}+1 as

δi≜wage​(Δk)​α​ρiclip​(rt,islow,k−rt,ifast,bl),\delta_{i}\;\triangleq\;w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta_{k})\,\alpha\,\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i}\,\bigl(r^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i}-r^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}_{t,i}\bigr), (1)

with non-negative age kernel wage​(Δ)≥0w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta)\!\geq\!0 (Theorem 2.1 holds for any choice that preserves row-stochasticity of the resulting delay kernel Λ\Lambda). We adopt wage​(Δ)=γΔw_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta){=}\gamma^{\Delta} with γ=exp(−1/τage)\gamma{=}\exp(-1/\tau_{\mathrm{age}}), τage=1000\tau_{\mathrm{age}}{=}1000, near-unity over the operating Δ\Delta-grid; Appendix C ablates this choice (Table 3). Global gain α>0\alpha>0 (default α=1\alpha{=}1), and V-trace-style clipped importance ratio ρiclip=min⁡(ρ¯,πθt+Δ+1​(at,i)/πθt​(at,i))\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i}=\min(\bar{\rho},\pi_{\theta_{t+\Delta+1}}(a_{t,i})/\pi_{\theta_{t}}(a_{t,i})) with ρ¯=1\bar{\rho}{=}1 default; the clip bounds the per-step ratio between the current actor and the actor that originally generated the rollout, following the standard off-policy correction used in V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018). The advantage fed to the policy-gradient update is A~i=Ai+δi\widetilde{A}_{i}=A_{i}+\delta_{i}. The correction is applied to the next optimiser step and never modifies a previously committed gradient. When the forward-injection mechanism is disabled the update reduces exactly to vanilla PPO/GRPO.

Cumulative unbiasedness.

Theorem 2.1 (Cumulative bias of RAC).

Define the effective delay kernel

Λ~​[k,Δ]≜α​wage​(Δ)​Λ​[k,Δ],\widetilde{\Lambda}[k,\Delta]\;\triangleq\;\alpha\,w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta)\,\Lambda[k,\Delta],

where α>0\alpha\!>\!0 is the global gain, wage:ℕ→[0,1]w_{\mathrm{age}}\!:\!\mathbb{N}\!\to\![0,1] is the non-negative age kernel, Λ⁡[k,Δ]∈[0,1]\Lambda[k,\Delta]\!\in\![0,1] is the probability that channel kk’s reward is delayed by exactly Δ∈{0,…,D}\Delta\!\in\!\{0,\dots,D\} optimiser steps, and DD is the maximum admissible delay. For each channel kk, let

ηk≜ 1−∑Δ=0DΛ~​[k,Δ]∈[0,1]\eta_{k}\;\triangleq\;1-\textstyle\sum_{\Delta=0}^{D}\widetilde{\Lambda}[k,\Delta]\;\in\;[0,1]

denote the sub-stochasticity slack of row kk of Λ~\widetilde{\Lambda} (non-negative since α​wage​(Δ)≤α\alpha\,w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta)\!\leq\!\alpha and ∑ΔΛ⁡[k,Δ]≤1\sum_{\Delta}\Lambda[k,\Delta]\!\leq\!1, so each row sums to at most one at α≤1\alpha\!\leq\!1). Suppose, for every delay Δ\Delta:

  • •

    (U) Conditionally mean-one clipped IS ratio. 𝔼[ρt,Δ,iclip∣st,i,at,i]=1\mathbb{E}[\rho_{t,\Delta,i}^{\mathrm{clip}}\mid s_{t,i},a_{t,i}]\!=\!1 under the behaviour distribution. This is the standard V-trace truncation condition (Espeholt et al., 2018); it holds exactly at the identity actor and approximately under V-trace clipping with bounded policy drift.

  • •

    (CI) Conditional independence. Conditional on (st,i,at,i)(s_{t,i},a_{t,i}), the clipped importance ratio ρt,Δ,iclip\rho_{t,\Delta,i}^{\mathrm{clip}} is independent of the slow-minus-fast residual rt,islow,k−rt,ifast,blr^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i}\!-\!r^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}_{t,i} (which does not depend on Δ\Delta).

Then, for each channel kk, the cumulative RAC correction satisfies

𝔼⁡[∑tδt,i]=(1−ηk)​∑t(𝔼​rt,islow,k−𝔼​rt,ifast,bl),\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{t}\delta_{t,i}\Bigr]\;=\;(1-\eta_{k})\,\textstyle\sum_{t}\bigl(\mathbb{E}\,r^{\mathrm{slow},k}_{t,i}-\mathbb{E}\,r^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}_{t,i}\bigr), (2)

where δt,i\delta_{t,i} is channel kk’s reinjected correction (Equation 1). The correction is exactly unbiased (ηk=0\eta_{k}\!=\!0) iff the effective row sums to one, condition (R): ∑Δ=0DΛ~​[k,Δ]=1\sum_{\Delta=0}^{D}\widetilde{\Lambda}[k,\Delta]\!=\!1. Condition (R) holds at the V-trace identity kernel Λ=I\Lambda\!=\!I (where wage​(0)=1w_{\mathrm{age}}(0)\!=\!1, α=1\alpha\!=\!1), and at a saturated kernel Λ[k,Δ]=𝟙{Δ=Δ¯k}\Lambda[k,\Delta]\!=\!\mathbb{1}\{\Delta\!=\!\bar{\Delta}_{k}\} under the row-normalisation α=1/wage​(Δ¯k)\alpha\!=\!1/w_{\mathrm{age}}(\bar{\Delta}_{k}); otherwise the residual bias is linear in the slack ηk\eta_{k}.

Theorem 2.1 bounds the cumulative correction by a factor (1−η)(1-\eta) of the synchronous-reward-pipeline target: at the row-stochastic kernel (η=0\eta\!=\!0) the correction is exact, and the bias grows linearly with the row-stochasticity slack elsewhere. The identity is algebraic in (δi,Λ~,ρclip)(\delta_{i},\widetilde{\Lambda},\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}): it does not depend on the policy parameterisation, the state-action space, or the optimiser. Any PPO, GRPO, or downstream method that applies to the corrected advantage A~i=Ai+δi\widetilde{A}_{i}=A_{i}+\delta_{i} inherits this cumulative-bias identity. At the identity kernel Λ=I\Lambda{=}I the statement collapses to V-trace’s on-policy guarantee (Espeholt et al., 2018); the contribution is the multi-channel Δ\Delta-lagged forward-injection. We verify the collapse empirically at 77B scale: on N=500N{=}500 UltraFeedback prompts scored by Qwen2.52.5-77B (fast head) and Skywork-Llama-3.13.1-88B (slow oracle), the max element-wise difference between the RAC and V-trace advantages at Λ=I\Lambda{=}I, ρclip=1\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}{=}1, with the identity baseline rfast,bl=rfastr^{\mathrm{fast,bl}}{=}r^{\mathrm{fast}}, is 00 in float-6464 (Appendix G). The full proof, together with a Monte-Carlo validation that recovers exact zero bias in every row-stochastic cell and the predicted linear slack in a non-row-stochastic control, is given in Appendix B.

Per-step total-variation bound.

Proposition 2.2 (Per-step total-variation bound for RAC-corrected policies).

Let πt\pi_{t} and π~t\widetilde{\pi}_{t} denote the fast-only policy and the RAC-corrected policy at optimiser step tt, respectively. Suppose:

  • •

    (A1) Bounded clipped IS ratio. There exists ρ¯<∞\bar{\rho}\!<\!\infty with ρiclip≤ρ¯\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{clip}}\!\leq\!\bar{\rho} almost surely.

  • •

    (A2) Bounded slow-residual variance. The slow-channel residual has variance bounded uniformly by σs2<∞\sigma_{s}^{2}\!<\!\infty across (t,k,i)(t,k,i).

  • •

    (A3) Finite per-step KL. The per-step Kullback–Leibler divergence KLt≜𝔼[KL(πt∥π~t)]\mathrm{KL}_{t}\!\triangleq\!\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{t}\|\widetilde{\pi}_{t})] is finite.

Then the state-averaged total-variation distance between the two policies at step tt, TV¯t≜𝔼sTV(πt∥π~t∣s)\overline{\mathrm{TV}}_{t}\!\triangleq\!\mathbb{E}_{s}\mathrm{TV}(\pi_{t}\|\widetilde{\pi}_{t}\mid s), is bounded by

TV¯t≤min⁡{12​KLt, 1−12​exp⁡(−KLt)}.\overline{\mathrm{TV}}_{t}\;\leq\;\min\!\Bigl\{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}_{t}},\;1-\tfrac{1}{2}\exp(-\mathrm{KL}_{t})\Bigr\}. (3)

The bound is the pointwise minimum of Pinsker’s inequality (Canonne, 2022) and the Bretagnolle–Huber lemma (Bretagnolle & Huber, 1979). The Pinsker branch is tighter for KLt<KL∗\mathrm{KL}_{t}\!<\!\mathrm{KL}^{*} and the Bretagnolle–Huber branch is tighter for KLt>KL∗\mathrm{KL}_{t}\!>\!\mathrm{KL}^{*}, where the crossover point KL∗≈1.6259\mathrm{KL}^{*}\!\approx\!1.6259 is the unique positive root of 12​KL=1−12​exp⁡(−KL)\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}}\!=\!1-\tfrac{1}{2}\exp(-\mathrm{KL}).

The proof is in Appendix A.

Composability and scope.

RAC integrates with any reward-manager exposing the standard PPO/GRPO interface (Sheng et al., 2024; von Werra et al., 2020) through a two-line patch: an O⁡(K)O(K) queue update and a single tensor addition per optimiser step. Wall-clock overhead on a 1.51.5B Qwen2.5 PPO run sits within Monte-Carlo noise of vanilla GRPO. The policy-gradient objective, the KL regulariser, and the rest of the advantage estimator are unchanged; the only modification is the additive correction A~i=Ai+δi\widetilde{A}_{i}=A_{i}+\delta_{i}. Code, configurations, regression probes, and the closed-form NumPy benchmark are released at the repository linked in §1.

3 Empirical Demonstration

Setup.

The benchmark is a 33-state ×\times 22-action tabular MDP with a known ground-truth reward, a fast channel that adds Gaussian noise 𝒩⁡(0,σf2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{f}^{2}) with σf=0.5\sigma_{f}{=}0.5, and KK slow channels with independent delays Δk∈{1,…,5}\Delta_{k}\in\{1,\dots,5\} matching the ground-truth signal. We measure the policy-level ℓ2\ell_{2} bias of the induced policy against the optimal policy, averaged over 5050 MDP seeds with 10001000 trials per seed, and report per-KK bootstrap 95%95\% confidence intervals (number of bootstrap resamples B=1000B{=}1000).

K=2K{=}2 result and cost-quality Pareto.

K=2K{=}2 corresponds to the canonical async-RLHF deployment with two slow channels (typically a code-execution verifier and a slow judge-RM ensemble) running alongside a fast PRISM-style scorer (Kirk et al., 2024). Table 1 confirms Theorem 2.1’s prediction: at K=2K{=}2 RAC reduces the closed-form policy bias by 47.9×\bm{47.9\times} (top block). The saturated row-stochastic kernel reaches 48.3×48.3\times. The baseline-comparison block isolates the cost-quality tradeoff: wait-for-slow reaches 27.1×27.1\times but pays the full 𝔼⁡[Δ]\mathbb{E}[\Delta] wall-clock penalty per training step (26×26\times relative to naive), and Retrace at the advantage level (Munos et al., 2016) collapses to 1.5×1.5\times because its γΔ\gamma^{\Delta} kernel strips most of the slow signal at the operating Δ\Delta grid. RAC sits at (1×, 47.9×)(1{\times},\,47.9\times) on the cost-quality plane, achieving higher bias-reduction at lower wall-clock cost than wait-for-slow, and higher reduction than Retrace-A at near-equal cost (Figure 2).

Cross-topology 𝑲=𝟐\bm{K{=}2} replication.

A cross-topology KK-sweep replicates the K=2K{=}2 configuration on all five tabular topologies (median reduction 21.7×21.7\times; full grid in Appendix C).

Scope of the closed-form result.

Theorem 2.1 and the 47.9×47.9\times figure are derived on a tabular MDP with known ground truth, where the unbiasedness identity is most legible; the peak sits at the upper end of an order-of-magnitude MDP-structure spread (Appendix F), so we treat it as a proof-of-concept. At 77B scale the underlying algebra holds to machine precision on real reward distributions (Appendix G).

4 Conclusion

RAC is a closed-form forward-injection primitive for delay-aware RLHF: a cumulative-unbiasedness identity that recovers V-trace at the identity kernel, a 47.9×\bm{47.9\times} closed-form peak bias reduction at K=2K{=}2 at lower wall-clock cost than wait-for-slow, and a two-line patch on any PPO/GRPO reward-manager. Its scope is the theorem, the tabular proof-of-concept, and a static-batch 77B probe that confirms the algebra to machine precision; end-to-end LLM-scale PPO validation is the next experimental step.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 2.2 (TV Bound)

Proposition 2.2 composes Pinsker’s inequality with the Bretagnolle–Huber lemma. Pinsker (Canonne, 2022) states TV(π∥π~)≤12KL(π∥π~)\mathrm{TV}(\pi\|\widetilde{\pi})\leq\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\widetilde{\pi})}; Bretagnolle & Huber (1979) states TV(π∥π~)≤1−12exp(−KL(π∥π~))\mathrm{TV}(\pi\|\widetilde{\pi})\leq 1-\tfrac{1}{2}\exp(-\mathrm{KL}(\pi\|\widetilde{\pi})). The composite bound is the pointwise minimum, and the crossover point is the unique root of 12​KL−(1−12​exp⁡(−KL))=0\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}}-(1-\tfrac{1}{2}\exp(-\mathrm{KL}))=0 on [0,∞)[0,\infty) (numerical root KL∗≈1.6259\mathrm{KL}^{*}\!\approx\!1.6259). Both inequalities hold per state ss; assumptions (A1)-(A2) bound the clipped ratio and the slow-residual variance so that the per-state KL is finite, and (A3) makes its state average KLt\mathrm{KL}_{t} finite. Averaging the per-state Pinsker bound and applying Jensen’s inequality to the concave map x↦xx\!\mapsto\!\sqrt{x} gives 𝔼s​[12​KL​(s)]≤12​𝔼s​KL​(s)=12​KLt\mathbb{E}_{s}[\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}(s)}]\!\leq\!\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{s}\mathrm{KL}(s)}\!=\!\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{KL}_{t}}; the Bretagnolle–Huber branch averages directly, yielding Equation 3. A Monte-Carlo sweep across three KL settings on the canonical-MDP benchmark shows the composite bound is empirically loose by an order of magnitude at small KL but never violated, with Bretagnolle–Huber tight in the large-KL regime while Pinsker becomes vacuous. The empirical reduction under RAC is reported in Table 1.

Appendix C Cross-Topology K-Sweep and Ablations

The cross-topology K-sweep covers five tabular topologies (canonical 3×23{\times}2, chain 5×25{\times}2, cyclic 4×34{\times}3, dense 5×35{\times}3, terminal 3×23{\times}2), seven KK-values, five MDP seeds, three Monte-Carlo seeds, and 30003000 trials per cell (≈1.6×106\approx\!1.6{\times}10^{6} trajectories total). The grid uses an artificial per-channel decomposition rk=rtotal/K+εkr_{k}=r_{\mathrm{total}}/K+\varepsilon_{k} with εk∼𝒩⁡(0,0.32)\varepsilon_{k}\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,0.3^{2}) and the KK-th noise term pinned to εK=−∑k<Kεk\varepsilon_{K}\!=\!-\sum_{k<K}\varepsilon_{k} to preserve channel-sum invariance ∑krk=rtotal\sum_{k}r_{k}\!=\!r_{\mathrm{total}}, and deterministic per-channel delay Δk=k\Delta_{k}{=}k. Table 2 and Figure 5 report per-topology argmax-KK, the 5%5\%-tolerance peak-band, reduction at argmax, and reduction at K=15K{=}15.

Retrace-A baseline adaptation.

The Retrace-A comparator (Table 1 bottom block) applies the Munos et al. (2016) clipped importance ratio ρiclip\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i} to the slow-residual reward injected at optimiser step t+Δk+1t{+}\Delta_{k}{+}1 (not to the value-function target as in the original Retrace formulation), with a γΔ\gamma^{\Delta} geometric age-decay in place of RAC’s exp(−Δ/τage)\exp(-\Delta/\tau_{\mathrm{age}}) kernel. We instantiate the discount with the standard RL value γ=0.5\gamma{=}0.5 to mirror typical TD(λ\lambda) tabular-MDP settings, not RAC’s near-unity γ=exp(−1/τage)\gamma{=}\exp(-1/\tau_{\mathrm{age}}); the corresponding γΔ\gamma^{\Delta} at Δ∈{1,…,5}\Delta{\in}\{1,\ldots,5\} sits in {0.5,0.25,0.125,0.0625,0.03125}\{0.5,0.25,0.125,0.0625,0.03125\}, which strips the slow signal at the operating grid and produces the reported 1.5×1.5\times collapse. Substituting RAC’s age-discount γ=exp(−1/τage)\gamma{=}\exp(-1/\tau_{\mathrm{age}}) into Retrace-A recovers the bare-additive 27.1×27.1\times floor; the remaining gap between bare-additive and RAC’s 47.9×47.9\times is the contribution of the IS clip plus the row-stochastic-kernel forward-injection structure (Table 1 top-block knob ablation; reduction without wagew_{\mathrm{age}} is also 27.1×27.1\times).

Cross-topology summary.

Across all five topologies, the per-topology argmax KK falls in {3,5}\{3,5\} and the K=2K{=}2 bias-reduction holds in the 8.98.9–34.5×34.5\times range (median 21.7×21.7\times). The closed-form guarantee does not extend to function-approximation or deep-policy settings where the ground-truth optimal policy is unavailable.

Knob ablations at K=2K{=}2.

Table 3 ablates the age kernel and the IS clip at K=2K{=}2, averaged over Δ∈{5,20,50}\Delta\!\in\!\{5,20,50\}. Removing the age kernel (τage→∞\tau_{\mathrm{age}}{\to}\infty, so wage≡1w_{\mathrm{age}}{\equiv}1) drops the reduction from 47.9×47.9\times to 27.1×27.1\times. Removing the IS clip on top yields the same 27.1×27.1\times, since the closed-form benchmark uses an identity actor with ρ=1\rho{=}1; the clip becomes load-bearing once a drifting actor enters the picture (Appendix D).

Appendix D Heavy-Tailed Delay-Distribution Stress

The K=2K{=}2 47.9×47.9\times result uses deterministic per-trajectory delay Δ\Delta, while production asynchronous RLHF returns heavy-tailed slow-RM latencies (queue contention, batch jitter, GPU evictions). This stress test asks whether the K=2K{=}2 RAC bias-reduction at matched mean delay 𝔼⁡[Δ]=20\mathbb{E}[\Delta]{=}20 holds when Δ\Delta is drawn per-trajectory from progressively heavier-tailed distributions.

Five distributions are matched at 𝔼⁡[Δ]=20\mathbb{E}[\Delta]{=}20 (Figure 4) so that any divergence isolates tail shape, not mean. The distributions are deterministic (Δ≡20\Delta\equiv 20), clipped Gaussian (clip⁡(round⁡(𝒩⁡(20,62)),1,200)\mathrm{clip}(\mathrm{round}(\mathcal{N}(20,6^{2})),1,200)), lognormal (μ=ln⁡20−σ2/2\mu=\ln 20-\sigma^{2}/2, σ=0.5\sigma=0.5), Pareto-finite (α=3\alpha=3, xm=23⋅20x_{m}=\tfrac{2}{3}\!\cdot\!20, finite mean and variance), and truncated-Cauchy (median 1818, scale 44, truncated to [1,200][1,200]). The full design crosses five MDP seeds with three Monte-Carlo seeds, five distributions, three τage\tau_{\mathrm{age}} levels, 10001000 trials per cell, and T=50T{=}50 optimiser steps, yielding 2.25×1052.25{\times}10^{5} trajectories overall. We use an identity actor with ρ=1\rho{=}1 and αδ=1\alpha_{\delta}{=}1 to match the closed-form K=2K{=}2 benchmark.

Realised distributions and scope.

The [1,200][1,200] clip neuters Pareto’s heavy tail in second-moment terms, so the substantive claim is robustness to the realised truncated distributions, not to unbounded heavy-tail variance. The truncated-Cauchy realised pooled mean is ≈21.0\approx\!21.0 (a 5%5\% shift above the 2020 target induced by the asymmetric tail under the [1,200][1,200] clip); the other four distributions match the target to within 0.01%0.01\%. The experiment uses an identity actor and IID per-trajectory Δ\Delta; burst-correlated delays and adaptive τage\tau_{\mathrm{age}} controllers are out of scope.

Appendix E Limitations and Discussion

Closed-form scope.

The 47.9×47.9\times bias-reduction and Theorem 2.1’s exact unbiasedness identity are derived under a closed-form tabular MDP with a row-stochastic delay-kernel configuration. Off saturation, the bias slack scales with the deviation from row-stochasticity, validated linearly across ∑ΔΛ∈{0.95,0.90,0.85,0.80,0.70,0.50}\sum_{\Delta}\Lambda\in\{0.95,0.90,0.85,0.80,0.70,0.50\} (Appendix B). The five-topology K-sweep covers four further tabular topologies in state-count, action-count, transition-density, and reward-sparsity but does not span the full tabular-MDP space, and the closed-form guarantee does not extend to linear-function-approximation or deep-policy settings.

Channel-count recommendation.

The cross-topology K-sweep (Appendix C) places the per-topology argmax at K∈{3,5}K\!\in\!\{3,5\}. Our recommended deployment setting is K=2K{=}2, the canonical async-RLHF configuration; the unbiasedness theorem is per-channel under the row-stochastic kernel and holds irrespective of KK.

LLM-scale validation.

The closed-form analysis assumes a two-channel setup: one slow ground-truth-grade verifier paired with one fast biased estimator. The 77B-scale checks (Appendices B and G) confirm that the algebra holds at real reward scale to machine precision. End-to-end LLM-scale PPO validation across multiple seeds and fast-RM training settings (random-init head, Bradley–Terry-trained head, production reward model) is the natural next experimental step; compute scope is discussed in the Conclusion.

Theorem-side scope.

Propositions 2.2 and 2.1 assume bounded slow-channel residual variance and bounded delay. These assumptions hold for bounded preference ratings, which is the setting we target. The unbounded-residual and unbounded-delay extensions are out of scope for the present work.

Background and discussion.

V-trace (Espeholt et al., 2018) and Retrace (Munos et al., 2016) are the canonical clipped IS correctors for off-policy value-function targets, both acting on the inner critic. RAC relocates the same truncation idea to the advantage level and addresses asynchronous-reward staleness within an actor’s rollout, not asynchronous-actor staleness between worker and learner. The operative distinction at the advantage level is that RAC’s forward-injection commits to step t+Δ+1t{+}\Delta{+}1 using the cached log-policy from step tt, with no re-sampled trajectory. V-trace would require importance-weighted truncation on a re-sampled rollout, and RAC pays for the cached-actor mismatch via the geometric age-discount in closed form (Theorem 2.1).

Replication notes.

The closed-form K=2K{=}2 tabular MDP benchmark reproduces in roughly 3030 lines of NumPy on a single CPU thread; the heavy-tail stress runs in ∼945\sim\!945 s on a single CPU thread for 2.25×1052.25{\times}10^{5} trajectories. The reward-manager patch is a two-line addition plus a queue-maintenance helper.

Appendix F MDP-Size Scaling

To probe whether the 47.9×47.9\times result is an artifact of the ×23\!\times\!2 tabular toy, we construct a family of MDPs with identical recipe (softmax transitions, Unif⁡(−0.5,0.5)\mathrm{Unif}(-0.5,0.5) fast reward, structured slow-channel bump on (s=0,a=|A|−1)(s{=}0,a{=}|A|{-}1) plus Unif⁡(−0.3,0.3)\mathrm{Unif}(-0.3,0.3) state-dependent jitter, γ=0.9\gamma{=}0.9) at sizes (|S|,|A|)∈{(3,2),(5,3),(10,5),(20,8)}(|S|,|A|)\!\in\!\{(3,2),(5,3),(10,5),(20,8)\}. Each MDP size is averaged over five MDP-structure seeds at the default RAC configuration, K=2K{=}2, Δ\Delta-grid {5,20,50}\{5,20,50\}, 1,0001{,}000 trials per cell (60,00060{,}000 trajectories per size cell).

Tables 5 and 6 place the 47.9×47.9\times peak of Table 1 at the upper end of a size-induced spread: the ×23\!\times\!2 mean over five MDP-structure seeds is 17.87×17.87\times (bootstrap 95%95\% CI [11.31,26.05][11.31,26.05], B=10,000B{=}10{,}000), and the mean reduction softens monotonically to 4.65×4.65\times at ×820\!\times\!8 while the per-cell minimum remains above 3.99×3.99\times. The within-size spread also shrinks with size: Theorem 2.1 addresses expectations only (per-channel, independent of |S|⋅|A||S|\!\cdot\!|A|), and the narrowing of the within-size box is a separate empirical observation that the trajectory-level Monte-Carlo variance shrinks with the state-action support. We summarise the result as an order-of-magnitude reduction (4.654.65–17.9×17.9\times mean) across MDPs in {3,5,10,20}\{3,5,10,20\} states.

Appendix G Static-Batch Advantage-Quality Probe at 7B

Motivation and setup.

To probe whether the K=2K{=}2 closed-form 47.9×\bm{47.9\times} result (Table 1) carries to real reward signals on real text, we test the static advantage-estimator quality, decoupled from PPO training dynamics: a single fixed policy generates N=500N{=}500 greedy responses to UltraFeedback test-split prompts using Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and each (prompt, response) is scored with both reward channels. The fast channel is a random-init Linear(h,1)(h,1) scoring head over Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct’s last-token hidden state, seeded for reproducibility (matches the TwoChannelRewardModule fast-RM construction used elsewhere in this paper). The slow channel is Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B-v0.2 with its native scalar reward head, the trained oracle. Both RMs run 4-bit nf4 with bf16 compute on a single H100. For each delay channel we sample one delay per step and construct three advantage sequences over t=0,…,499t{=}0,\dots,499: Async=rslow−blA_{\mathrm{sync}}{=}r_{\mathrm{slow}}{-}\mathrm{bl} (synchronous oracle), Acontrol=rfast−blA_{\mathrm{control}}{=}r_{\mathrm{fast}}{-}\mathrm{bl} (delayed-fast, slow signal discarded), and ARAC=Acontrol+∑s:s+Δs=twage(Δs)(rsslow−rsfast)A_{\mathrm{RAC}}{=}A_{\mathrm{control}}+\sum_{s:\,s+\Delta_{s}=t}w_{\mathrm{age}}(\Delta_{s})(r^{\mathrm{slow}}_{s}{-}r^{\mathrm{fast}}_{s}) (RAC forward-injection, τage=1000\tau_{\mathrm{age}}{=}1000, identity actor ρ=1\rho{=}1 under fixed-policy). The running-mean baseline is causal in tt.

Results.

Table 6 reports two metrics: ℓ2\ell_{2} error against the oracle (‖A∗−Async‖2\|A_{\mathrm{*}}{-}A_{\mathrm{sync}}\|_{2}) and cosine similarity to the oracle. Figure 7 visualises the same numbers.

Identity-kernel collapse at LLM scale.

On the same N=500N{=}500 scored (rfast,rslow)(r^{\mathrm{fast}},r^{\mathrm{slow}}) pairs used above (Llama-33-88B greedy generations, random-init Qwen2.5-7B fast head with seed 4242, Skywork-Llama-3.13.1-88B slow oracle), we evaluate the identity-kernel special case of Theorem 2.1. With Λ=I\Lambda{=}I (zero delay, one-hot kernel), wage​(0)=1w_{\mathrm{age}}(0){=}1, and clipped IS ratio ρclip=1\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}{=}1 (frozen policy), the RAC advantage ARAC=rfast+ρclip​wage​(0)​(rslow−rfast)−blA_{\mathrm{RAC}}{=}r^{\mathrm{fast}}{+}\rho^{\mathrm{clip}}\,w_{\mathrm{age}}(0)\,(r^{\mathrm{slow}}{-}r^{\mathrm{fast}}){-}\mathrm{bl} algebraically collapses to V-trace’s on-policy advantage AV​-​trace=rslow−blA_{\mathrm{V\text{-}trace}}{=}r^{\mathrm{slow}}{-}\mathrm{bl}. Computing both quantities via independent code paths on the same causal running-mean baseline and comparing element-wise yields ‖ARAC−AV​-​trace‖∞=0.0\|A_{\mathrm{RAC}}{-}A_{\mathrm{V\text{-}trace}}\|_{\infty}{=}0.0 in our float-6464 implementation (the algebra is exact in arithmetic; the empirical match reflects identical operation order across both code paths), confirming the identity-kernel collapse at 77B scale on real reward distributions.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
